Yash, you told me you keep correcting your grandfather. Let me tell you what I learned the hard way. When my mother's memory was going, she would put on her sari every morning at seven and say, "I'm late for school, the children are waiting." She had retired as a teacher twenty years before.
At first I argued. "Amma, you don't teach anymore!" She'd cry, then shout, then search the house for her register. Every morning, the same battle.
Then a nurse told me, "Don't fight the facts. Answer the feeling." So the next morning I said, "Your students were lucky. Tell me about them." She sat down with her tea and talked for an hour, smiling.
After that, we kept mornings calm: the same tea, the same chair, her old school photos nearby. The battles stopped.

Your uncle Pranav

A wedding band was blaring down the lane when Dadaji stood up at nine at night, pulling on his coat. "I'll miss the train to the office!"
"Dada, you retired years ago," Sachin said, exasperated.
Dadaji's hands started to shake. "Don't lie to me. They'll sack me."
Swati, twenty-five, caught her brother's eye and shook her head. She went to her grandfather and took his hand. "Dadaji, you always worked so hard. The train's late tonight. Let's have tea while we wait."
The drums grew louder. Swati closed the windows, drew the curtains and put on his favourite bhajan, soft. She sat him in his armchair and handed him his cup.
Slowly, his shoulders came down. "Late again," he muttered. "These railways." By the second cup, he was dozing.
Sachin whispered, "How did you do that?"
"I stopped arguing."

passage: When Nani Kalyani first came to live with us, I argued with her all the time. She'd say it was 1980, or that she had to catch a train to her mother's village, and I would correct her, patiently at first and then less patiently. She'd get upset and scared, and I'd feel awful. I'm Usha, and it took me months to understand that the facts weren't the point. When she said she needed to catch the train, she was really saying, 'I miss my mother. I feel lost.' So I started answering that. 'You're missing your Amma. Tell me about her village.' We built a routine: same chair, same tea at four, same old songs on the radio. Her distress dropped. She still gets muddled. But she's calmer, and so am I.
